entries.topicDescription: Type parameters, wildcards, and why generics are erased at runtime.

tips.title: Generics exist only at compile time — type erasure removes them at runtime
tips.content:
The compiler uses a class's type parameters to catch mismatches
at compile time, then erases them: List<String> and List<Integer>
compile down to the exact same List bytecode, with an
automatically-inserted cast wherever an element is read back out.

This is why you can't do 'new T[10]' or 'instanceof List<String>'
— at runtime there is no T, and no way to distinguish a
List<String> from a List<Integer> by type alone. It's also why
two overloaded methods differing only by generic type parameter
(process(List<String>) vs process(List<Integer>)) don't compile
— they'd erase to an identical signature.

Erasure exists for backward compatibility: generics were added
in Java 5, and erasure let generic code interoperate with
pre-generics bytecode compiled years earlier.

tips.title: PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Extends — reading wildcards
tips.content:
'? extends T' (an upper-bounded wildcard) means the collection
PRODUCES T values you can read, but you can't add to it — the
compiler can't know the exact runtime subtype, so any add()
could violate it. 'List<? extends Number>' could actually be a
List<Integer> at runtime; adding a Double to it would be unsafe.

'? super T' (a lower-bounded wildcard) means the collection
CONSUMES T values you can write into, but reads only come back
as Object, since the exact supertype is unknown. This is the
shape you want for an output parameter that just needs to accept
T and its subtypes.

The mnemonic is PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Extends...
no: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter only ever
gives you values, use extends; if it only ever receives values
from you, use super.

tips.title: Bounded type parameters let you call methods on T itself
tips.content:
A plain <T> gives you no information about T beyond "it's some
reference type" — you can't call any method on a T value except
the ones every Object has. A bounded type parameter, <T extends
Comparable<T>>, adds a constraint the compiler enforces at every
call site, and in exchange lets the method body call
compareTo() directly on a T.

Multiple bounds are allowed with '&' (T extends Comparable<T> &
Serializable), but at most one of them may be a class — the rest
must be interfaces, since Java has no multiple inheritance of
implementation.

This is the mechanism behind generic algorithms like
Collections.max(), which requires its element type to be
Comparable precisely so it can compare elements without knowing
their concrete type in advance.
